review:
It's a flawed game, and while I enjoy it I can't help but see the areas in which it fell short of its forebear.  This game isn't going to convert anyone; the same people who liked/hated State of Decay 1 will like/hate its sequel.  They took a lot of good ideas from the community, but can't escape a general bugginess and overall janky feeling that its systems give.


BREAKDOWN:
Base Management- Fantastic.  Far more detailed than the prequel, and with a noise system to give tactical weight to large populations and construction-rushing.  Outposts no longer blow up hordes, but they give personalized bonuses depending on type (power stations drain fuel to give your base power more efficiently than generators, houses give extra beds, restaurants/doctor's offices give food/meds per day, etc).

Survivor Management- Phenomenal.  Specializations can be taken for every skill- including non-combat ones like construction- and are more interesting than before.  Survivors also give individual pluses and minuses to morale, giving you a reason to exile people.  You also can't just indefinitely push off sleep anymore.

Scavenging- Improved.  Buildings no longer runneth over with rucksacks, giving a better feeling of scarcity and desperation.  The items you find tend to be more varied, and weapons you find are broken down by stats with very few just being straight upgrades of each other.

Zombies- Faster, although still never faster than player sprint speed.  This makes them an actual threat again.  Plague zombies have also been added, suddenly adding an ACTUAL threat of survivors being zombified, that can nonetheless be avoided if players are lucky or planned ahead (and move quickly).  Bloaters are more insidious, Screamers have just a fraction more time to be interrupted while also acting a little bit like sentries to throw spanners into your stealth runs, and armored zeds feel less game-y to fight.  Ferals and Juggernauts have been changed for the worse, though, with both now feeling like overlong healthbars that cheese game systems to purposely screw you about.

Combat- Pared down.  Stealth feels more tactical (takedowns are a little longer, making them more easily interrupted by nearby zeds without feeling too long), but combat took a massive hit with the removal of the shove/kick button.  For non-heavy weapons, you mostly just hack, slash, dodge, and execute.  For heavy weapons, you realize you can't predict whether a swing will move you forward or backward, realize your range is inexcusably short for that windup time, regret specializing in powerhouse to do it, and go back to other weapons.  Attacking also seems scripted, for lack of a better word.  Your survivor gets into range to do the attack, then goes through the entire pre-swing checklist as though they had been caught by surprise, like an amateur actor unsubtly following stage directions.  This frequently gets me hit by zombies, which wouldn't be such a big deal except for the plague zombies that infect you more and more with every hit, suddenly shifting the blood plague from "This is my fault, I shouldn't have gotten near them" to "I wish the game hadn't screwed me."

Difficulty- Much improved.  You have three options from normal to nightmare, and even the normal difficulty proves intense once the tutorial period's grace has worn off.  It does make the death spiral infuriatingly difficult to break out of, though, as even if you try to just focus on your base and building yourself back up, the infestations are only getting worse, your people are upset you're not hunting down more plague hearts, and the missions you're ignoring for lack of time or resources are having an effect on your group's morale.

Exploration- Excellent.  Cars have fuel gauges now, and both fuel and damage can be restored with items that can be carried on your person or in the trunk.  Getting overly damaged or running out of fuel on a long trip leads to fantastic organic gameplay as you stop what you're doing to scavenge more.

Missions- The missions are great; varied and less frustrating than SoD 1.  The invisible timer on picking up missions, however, is entirely too short and I have missed some because one of those fantastic organic moments was busy happening on the other side of the map.  It's made more frustrating when missing missions can lower morale or cause entire enclaves to declare they're taking their ball and going home to never be seen again.  The game also seems to take a railroad-ey view of missions; in many cases, it seems to have already decided the way a mission will start and/or end, and you will find the rug pulled out from under you regardless of effort.  The game wants your mission to end in failure, so you return to watch a horde of plague zombies spawn one-by-one outside the door of your target, who break inside and turn them all in three-to-five hits.  A survivor needs an infestation to clear, so rather than waiting for an infestation to spawn naturally, the game spawns one regardless (and treats it as though you let the infestation happen, infuratingly)- in one case spawning an infestation inside an allied enclave's home, INSIDE THE SAFE ZONE OF A NEIGHBORING OUTPOST.  In all of these cases, the game persists in trying to blame you for this, which never fails to annoy.

NPCs- The AI is awful some of the time, but not all of the time.  I posit this is worse than the alternative, as it suckers you in just long enough to get reliant on it before a follower gets killed because he was stuck running into a wall, or you miss a zombie horde because your passenger decided he didn't want to open his door to hit them this time.  There is also special mention for the AI's reaction to plague zombies, in that it does not have one; the AI will persist in all its normal routines, oblivious to the fact that it is charging into a plague zombie horde while nearly infected.  

Enclaves- Interaction with other survivors outside your base is much improved.  Outside the same "you're the only one who seems to be willing to help these neighbors out" issue from SoD 1, you also have the ability to fight and kill humans.  You can threaten enclaves to make them give you what you want, and several missions have grey moral choices that can result in you slaughtering your fellow man so they can't pose a threat again or trying to forgive and forget.  Your morality can range from the usual messiah to a standard Walking Dead villain.

Polish- The game is buggy, but with the addition of an Unstuck command in the radio menu, it was never gamebreaking in-and-of itself.  Zombie hordes have a bad habit of spawning in rocks and interfering with AI, as in one case where I couldn't speak with a survivor to continue a mission I was on because she was busily trying to flank three unreachable zombies just outside my base.  And while I cannot prove it, I SUSPECT the devs tied durability to framerate.  My cars and weapons seem to be far more tissue paper than steel.

Spawning- The BIG issue.  The devs switched to spawning zeds in a bubble around you, with pacing dictated by a L4D-style AI director.  What this means is that zeds become tedious and routine as you can always count on a few being around regardless of your surroundings, unless you've just cleared an area.  Even then, the game will frequently spawn more zeds in areas you've just cleared once your back is turned, as noise no longer just attracts existing zombies, but also SPAWNS NEW ONES BEHIND OUT OF YOUR VIEW, meaning you can't even plan to clear an area out and expect it to be safe while the marker is telling you it's still safe.


In all, they improved more than they backslid, but the things they backslid on are things impacting more moment-to-moment issues.  The combat is a constant factor, while the glorious basebuilding is an infrequent pleasure.  These all combine to make a product roughly on-par with its forebear.  This is a very iffy recommendation, but a recommendation nonetheless.

Good game, but [b]BUYER BE WARNED if you are looking for a co-op experience[/b] with a friend / friend group / significant other.

Why it's bad:

Short version: Only the host can progress in the game, the clients get virtually nothing relevant to long-term progression.

Long version: To explain why this is bad, I will explain the basic gameplay loop.
1) Explore around the map and look for items, resources, survivors, or complete quests.
2) Return to your base with your loot / survivors.
3) Upgrade your base / craft stuff / using your resources

During step 1, you will get experience for your active survivor, leveling up their skills. You will get reputation, which is a currency which you can use to do lots of things, from upgrading stuctures, to recruiting survivors, to calling in airdrops of supplies. During step 3, you get to choose which buildings you want to build / upgrade, and you will chose based on which bonuses you want to give your settlement.

For co-op clients in this game, you cannot acquire resources. You cannot acquire survivors. You cannot complete quests. You do get items such as guns and bandages, however. You do get experience, so your survivors can level up. However, if your survivor dies in co-op, they are dead no matter if you are the host or the client, but because you cannot recruit new survivors as a client... maybe you see where this is going. You can very quickly run out of survivors with no way to replenish them. Or, even if you don't have them die, you can't get new ones, so you're stuck with just whoever you had to start with, forever.

As a client, you cannot upgrade the base. You cannot use most of the base facilities. You cannot take over outposts. You cannot use the outposts to learn new skills or receive any bonuses. You do not receive any bonuses from any of the base structures, such as passive health regeneration and so forth.

What does this all mean? What it ends up meaning is that, [b]if you are used to playing a game where 1 person hosts and everyone else joins, you will have a terrible f******g time playing this game[/b]. The host will have a normal experience, the clients will have a god-awful experience because they get basically nothing from playing. They will be using the same 3 starter people for the entire game and they will be p**s-poor at surviving because they don't get any of the passives from the base, they never rank up in standing with their own communities (so they don't get their powerful passives), and if they all die, that's it, your save file is deleted.

The only way you can circumvent this is to either have the clients play the game solo on their own time, so they can actually make progress, or to rotate who is hosting, so you can take turns progressing.

It's an absolutely bizarre game decision that only exists to solve the problem of having random public internet people join your game and mess with stuff, which is something I've never done, never wanted to do, and never had any desire to have happen, so the fact that all these 'protections' are put in place to prevent clients from interacting with the host's world is quite disappointing.

Good solo game tho.

This game has so much potential and I want to love it, but there's just so many things that make it incredibly frustrating.
First off, the good: the early game is incredibly fun, searching for supplies, killing zombies, building your base. It has a very Walking Dead feel and the combat is incredibly satisfying, especially due to the great animations. 

The somewhat good, somewhat bad: character customization is lacking on the one hand (you can't create characters, just pick from randomly generated ones), but you can customize their outfits at least and leveling them and watching them become stronger by improving their skills is fun. Base building and exploration is fun for a while, until you realize how extremely limited it is. You get to unlock all these nice new buildings by completing the legacy arcs or recruiting survivors with the right skills, but then even the biggest base locations have so few spots, that you can only build a few of those. And you can also only recruit a small number of survivors (12), which leads me to 

the bad: endgame is SEVERELY lacking. Once you built your base and recruited the maximum number of survivors, there's really not much to do. You clear the map of plague hearts and finish your leader's story and that's it. Once you finish a leader's legacy arc, your game ends, you cannot keep playing your community and have to start over. There is not really an open-end sandbox mode, unless of course you ignore the main missions, but there's so little to do after a while, that it just get's repetitive. You basically just keep defending against random zombie attacks on your base, which usually takes between 1 and 2 minutes, clear the randomly popping up infestations (which takes about 1 minute) or do the same missions for random NPCs over and over (mostly driving them from A to B, giving them some resources or clearing a location for them). 
There is an achievement in the game for lasting 100 days in one of the 2 higher difficulty modes (they're not that difficult, "normal" is basically casual mode anyway), but after less than 10 days the repetition will probably already set in. So this achievement isn't difficult, but it's still hard to get, because the boredom will probably take over before you get even close to it.

And then there's the bugs. Oh boy. I've lost track of the number of cars I've lost due to the buggy physics engine. Hit a small obstacle and if you're unlucky your car get's launched into the air, never to be seen again. Especially frustrating if you've got some good stuff in the trunk. And there's tons of other bugs, like missions being impossible to complete, because you have to kill all remaining zombies in an area, but then one or a few get stuck under the floor and you can't reach them, so you can't complete the mission. 

With mods I definitely had a somewhat fun time with the game, the early game is pretty cool, but what really makes this game a huge disappointment in the end, is the lack of proper endgame, balancing and more customization options (like bigger bases and communities).

In a sentence: this is the best zombie-survival game I have ever played, with hands-down the best dev team of the genre.

It was day 27 of the zombie apocalypse, and I was taking my favorite character out for scavenging. I'd recently ran out of gas, so I decided, what the heck, I'll just run to the nearest potential gas site... over half a kilometer away. This may not sound that far to you, but in the zombie apocalypse, half a kilometer on foot is like the journey your grandparents traveled to and from school back in their day: uphill both ways, in 5 feet of snow, with only a raw potato for lunch. But I'm no dummy. So before heading out, I grabbed a vial of plague cure, along with a bunch of stimulants, in case I happened to get into trouble...

Flash forward about 45 minutes. My favorite character is sprinting back to base, having contracted blood plague for a SECOND time this trip, after using up the one vial of plague cure I brought along. The timer at the bottom left of the screen is counting down the seconds until my guy drops dead from the plague. Meanwhile, there are three. Count. THREE Ferals (cat-like zombies that run on all fours and hate you and everyone you know) sprinting after me. My dude is downing stimulants like they're fricken Tic Tacs, while hauling butt back to base. He's bobbing and weaving like he's the star of a new Rocky movie, as these ferals hurl past him every couple seconds trying to slice through him like warm butter. But my guy has quads of steel, glutes that could crack open a walnut, and enough stimulants in him to kill a small country, so he just keeps on trucking. I'm on the edge of my seat, actively shouting at the screen, squeezing my controller to death, and implementing any other proven tactics I can think of for increasing the speed of my character.

Finally, I throw the door open to my base as my other community members gather to beat the ever-living heck out of these stupid ferals (it was a joyous moment). The timer has three seconds left on it as I down a vial of plague cure from my supply locker. My guy was safe. The relief I felt was better than having a scheduled phone call be canceled. Pure bliss.

The next day, my favorite character ran into a bloater while driving, contracted blood plague, and was then beaten into the ground by a Juggernaut. Devastation... like going over to a friend's house for a sleepover and realizing you forgot to bring an extra controller.

I will never forget you, favorite character, whose name has escaped me.


Thank you, Undead Labs, for giving me this experience. This is my favorite game of all-time! :)

The closest to my ideal post-zombie apocalypse game. Equal parts action, role-playing, base-building, and exploration.

A major wish would be that you could slowly reclaim the entire map, setting up multiple bases or forming alliances with other enclaves.

DO NOT BUY FOR MULTIPLAYER

My friends and I got this game to have something we could play together, but now we mostly play it by ourselves.
HERE'S WHY: The "Tethering" mechanic completely f*cks up the fun of multiplayer. You can only move 450m from the host before you get teleported back to them. In an Open World Game, this already stifles enjoyment a lot. 
That alone would be fine if you had something to do while you wait, but you don't.
The host is the only one who can expand the base and upgrade/use the different facilities. Exploring the map together is still enjoyable, but base management is an important part of this game, so it happens a lot. While the host is busy with that, you can explore maybe 5 locations near you, and once you've done that, you can only stand around. And the loot doesn't respawn or anything, so that way to pass the time only works the very first time you move to a new base.

TL;DR: Fun game, multiplayer should be fun, but isn't

State of Decay 2 is the true Zombie-Survival Game and I'll explain it in-depth for you. The following Review is Singleplayer-Only, but the Game has also Multiplayer-Coop where you can play with your Friends.

The Start of the Game:
It's the Zombie Apocalypse like you know from other Games, almost everybody have turned into Zombies and your Goal is to Survive with a Group of Humans. The Game features a detailed Base with Buildings and Facilities, that's your Home and the Goal of the Campagin Mode is simply to clear out each Plague Heart (some Kind of Bosses) on the Map, after that you'll complete a Storyline Quest which depends on your Leader of the Group. The Campaign Mode features 4 huge Maps.

The Team
Your Team starts with 3 random generated Characters, each comes with different Stats in Health, Stamina, Traits and Abilities. There are a lot of Traits, some are good and some are bad, for Example, a Sportsman which played Football in the College will have more Stamina and can run for a longer Time - a Lung Cancer Survivor on the other Hand will have a much lowered Stamina.

You got Skills for Fighting with Weapons or Guns. You can switch between the 3 and later more Survivors in your Team, when one is injured or tired, you take another one for playing on until the first one has recovered. You can later choose from more Skills in the Categorys, for example Specializing on Weapons, some are based on your Characters Traits.

You have a Backpack with max. 8 Slots, next to 2 Slots for a Melee-Weapon and a Gun. So be careful, what you take with you when going outside your Base: Will you take a Heal-Item more or better some Ammo? The Weight of the Items can slow you down, when carrying too much. It's like the old Resident Evil Style of Inventory, you'll have to choose carefully what you take with you. Items can be stored in your Base and you'll need empty Slots for getting new Items from Scavening.

For Survival, it is needed to get more Chars on your Team, which can be recruited by doing Missions for other AI controlled Survivors. Other Teams will show up on the Map and also try to surive, you can recruit them, trade with them or even kill them - be aware, they can also kill you when becoming Hostile.

Very Important: The Game has a Perma-Death-Feature. This means, when your Character gets killed, he's gone and you have to play on with another one - if all Chars in your Group died, you lose the Game.

Basic Gameplay:
Now, you start with Scavening your surrounding Area to get Resources: There are Food, Medicine, Ammo, Fuel and Materials. All those are needed, Food for Eating, Materials for Building your Base and so on. Each ingame-Day will need Resources, don't having them will give you Penaltys for Morale and Stamina (like when you starve because you lack food)

You can use Cars for Travelling on the Map, but they can take Damage and break down, so you'll need a Repair Kit. Also, you'll need Fuel to make them running. Note: A Car can be repaired even after Exploding, the Cars can always be recovered and the Items in the Trunk are not destroyed, so don't get in Panic when a Car goes up in Flames.

Combat:
The Zombies in SoD are blind, they react to Noise. A single Zombie can easily be killed by everybody, he's no Treat to you: But the Noise you make when knocking him down or shooting him, can and will attract other nearby Zombies, so you have to prevent a Chain-Reaction of Killing one Enemy and trigger a lot more Enemies while doing that. 

SoD features a lot of Weapons, from the simple Stick made of Wood to the Grenade Launcher, Guns are very efficient but also very noisy, even with Suppressors. 

Aside from regular Zombies, there are different Classes of Freaks, like a very fast Hunter called Feral, which you can't outrun. There's a very big one called Juggernaut which can be often avoided, but is difficult to fight. The Screamer will scream and call in every Zombie in the Area, the Bloater will walk right up to you and explode in a toxic Gas Cloud. These Freaks are very, very dangerous and can kill you quickly.

The real Danger comes from the Chain-Reaction, which can get you a Horde on your Back, Dozens of Zombies pursuing you until you escape or manage to kill them. You can throw Decoys like Sound-Effects to disturb them and draw them away from you to make things easier.

Base Management:
There's a lot of Options how to design your own Base and each Map features multiple Homesites. You can build Bed Shelters for Sleeping, a Garden for Harvesting Food, Watch- and Sniper-Tower for Defense, a Kitchen, Shooting Range and many other Buildings. Also, you can install Mods on the Facilities for various Effects.

The Zombies can and will siege your Base from Time to Time: This is depending on the Noise your Base makes, for Example, a Power-Generator will give you good Bonis, but the Noise will draw in Zombies faster and you'll need Fuel every day to keep it running. Buildings can be upgraded, for Example you can build a Auto-Repair Workshop to craft new Repair-Kits for Cars - but you'll need a Character in the Group with Mechanic Skills.


The Blood Plague:
The Game has a Feature called Blood Plague, when certain Zombies manage to bite you, you'll get infected. The Infection can be removed by a Hospital in your Base or by getting a Plague Cure. If the Infection reachs 100%, there will be Countdown-Timer (like 5 or 10 Minutes, depending on the Difficulty), if you don't heal your Char, he'll turn into a Zombie himself. To get the Cure, you'll need to hunt down Plague-Zombies or Plague-Hearts for Samples, which allows you to craft the Cure in your Hospital Facility.

The Missions:
You'll get Calls from other Survivors, which have their own Bases and there are a lot (!) of different Mission Types. Maybe the other Teams will require Food or other Resources, they will Trade or they'll assist you in getting down some Zombies and Plague-Hearts. Single Survivors will also call for Help or Assistance and can be often recruited later on. You also have a Radio, which allows you to ask other Survivors for Help, like Locating Resources or Call in Support.

The Gameplay with the various Difficulty Settings:
SoD changes in the Gameplay, the higher your Difficulty Setting is. On Easy (Green Zone) or Standard (Standard Zone), it's not very difficult - you'll have plenty of Resources and Survivors, Zombies are easy to kill and Base-Sieges easy to win. After playing a Map, your Survivor Chars will get into a Pool and you can choose 3 of them for starting a new Playthrough on another Map, even with their Inventory. 

You'll have to go Stealth even on Normal for not having always to Fight, you can Stealth-Kill Zombies from Behind and avoid Freaks by Sneaking around. After playing Normal, go on the higher Difficulties and look how far you get there, it becomes very hard. The Difficulty Settings can be made detailed by Sliders, for Example how much Resources there will be or how many Freaks, how dangerous the Zombies are etc.

The Final Rating:
The Perma-Death Feature makes you care a lot for your Chars in the Team, you'll bond to them and you'll do everything to keep them alive. Because of the random Chars, Maps with random Resource-Locations etc. you'll have 100% Replayability. There are many Options how you develop your Base and your Team, which Way you want to go, which Survivors you'll recruit and where you'll loot Locations.

So, when you get State of Decay: Make your Team, prepare your Base and get Resources, recruit new Members and mourn the dead Members of your Team, carry on and destroy all the Plague-Hearts to clear the Map, make your own Legacy and survive the Zombie-Apocalypse.

I can just recommend it, it is a very, very good Survival-Game which features different Things like Base Building, Perma-Death and Fighting in intense Battles against Hordes of Zombies.

Thumbs up or thumbs down? I only play SP, so it could have gone either way as SoD2 is a flawed gem. Why?

Let's start with the BIGGIE - the gameplay 'loop'. There is a sort of iterative pattern players have to go through with most games (grinding, levelling, exploring, building, upgrading etc etc) each cycle through you get tougher, better gear, more options etc. That is true to a degree with gear in this game but the loop in SOD2 for everything is both very shallow and short (pick up some gear - help an enclave - get a person - get a bigger base - repeat). What is worse, do this 3-4 times and you are done, 'end game' - at this point you either start fresh (new game) or move to a new map with a couple of your survivors and....start fresh. In essence, there is no end game, no ultimate goal, you just grind and struggle so you are allowed to reset the grind and struggle (albeit with a leader bonus and 3 experienced characters to start the next map - which is actually a negative because being a small, weak, easily overwhelmed group when you start is the most exciting and fun part of the game. 

Now the quirky stuff:
A tiny country village with a pre-apocalypse population of maybe 100 (going by the houses) has a zombie population of several times that - a zombie count that never decreases for any length of time no matter how many you kill. (this has had a patch to improve it but meh....still endless zombies re-spawning everywhere). 

A 4 door pick-up truck with a flat bed tray has 6 storage slots, each slot can be taken up by as little as 1 item - so your truck may be full if loaded down by 6 pieces of paper (which don't stack). A small backpack also has six slots ,also filled by 6 bits of unstackable paper, but it could also hold 6 fully automatic assault rifles if needed.

Some of the roadside curbs in Spencer's Mill (a town on one of the maps) need you to jump to go from the road to the footpath.

Wear and tear on equipment:A machete only 'works' for about 60 seconds of use, a kitchen knife driven repeatedly into human skulls works forever and ever and ever and ever.

AI is broken, it's just broken, followers refuse to fight (you die) or they refuse to stop fighting and run with you from unwinnable fights (they die). Replacing people in this game is slow, boring, frustrating and just generally painful. Replacing a skilled specialist is...(hmm, I don't have a civilised word for that, insert your own adjective here)

A fortified base designed in the apocalypse to protect survivors from zombie assault has 4 or 5 entry points, each 'blocked' by an unlockable, unreplacable and generally useless flimsy wire gate. Apparently 'fortification' and 'defensibility' are just long, meaningless, complicated words in this game world.

The game has cars. Great !!!! One such car is a Pilato - arguably the best all-round vehicle in the game - it's a mid-sized SUV largely 'comparable' to say a Chevrolet Traverse. Chevrolet tells me the Traverse has a gas tank that holds around 20 gallons (90 litres) of fuel and on highways gets about 26 miles per gallon ( about 9.3 km per litre) so a Traverse has a maximum range of about 520 miles (830 km) per tank. The Pilato has range of about 6-7 km per tank...that's 4.4 miles in the 'old money'. This kinda makes 'Dieselgate' look like a storm in a teacup. 

Heartland DLC, 6 hours into a game on easiest setting, 3 people in my base, just completed first story-line mission and my base was assault by 3 Juggernauts, 2 ferals, 4 screamers, 4 bloaters and what I think was about 30+ regular Zs - WTF is insane difficulty like?

My co-survivors CONSTANTLY complain about too many infestations - even when 90% of them are 2-3 km away on the other side of the map (they virtually reappear as quickly as you clear them) - who gives a s**t, we've got no food, no meds and 2 juggernauts patrolling our neighbourhood and you're worried about half a dozen Zeds setting up house in a ruined garage 3 km away ???!!! Go live somewhere else moron.

Radio: 'Emergency, please help us...we're in trouble.' You get there and there's 3 guys kitted out with machetes and guns standing around in a garage, they ask you (and your companion if you brought one) to go to location X and get them some food. It's the apocalypse, I'm looking for food as well, why should the ONE or TWO of us go into the infested house when you THREE gun-toting dudes won't? Toughen up princesses !!! Call me for help when your base is being overrun by a horde of ferals because you only used wire gates to block the entry points - like we all did apparently.

Missions flood in by radio. And I mean flood. Ignoring them loses you allies and/or damages morale. With your maximum 8 survivors you can only ever use 1 character (with optional companion) to do missions. It is literally impossible to help the whining, princess survivors all around you, clear infestations, deal with endlessly spawning hordes, repair and fuel vehicles, build the base, fix weapons and....so on. It's a shame, you feel like you are being constantly pushed into doing things you have no interest in doing when you really want to explore the map, hoard stuff, or whatever. Even taking the time to checkout the extensive wardrobe options for all the characters makes you feel like an ER doctor who just steps outside in the middle of an Earth-shattering crisis to update his/her Facebook page.

Finally, there is the 'base building' - hmm...copy-paste limited is a good description. Each map has only 5-7 base locations, these are all abandoned houses or commercial properties, each with a set number built-in (and unchangeable) facilities and a number of empty 'plots' which can be used to place a facility of your choice. After a while you get your favourite base locations which you want to use and build the facilities that suit your game play style, end result.....this play through's base looks and actually is identical to the last play through. Both the appearance of the base (survivors never clean out the debris and detritus) and the one-click-to-build process are super unfulfilling.  

There's a lot to like in this game (multiple maps, runs well, really beautiful to look at, good voice acting, atmospheric, solid animations and suitably gooey head splat sounds etc - and it's still getting significant content and gameplay updates which are improving most aspects of the game) but the above issues coupled with other problems (e.g., path finding and collision boxes) mean that for me the auto save dooms you to repeatedly wasting hours and hours of game-play only to have the game hit you with what seems like a stupendous moment from which you can only recover by significantly more hours of grinding (or easier if you are less than say...15 hours in, just start again). [h1]The TLDR version[/h1]
State of Decay 2 is essentially The Walking Dead + Rebuild - an open-world survival/sandbox community builder that feels unexpectedly like Civilization. I adore this game, it's a unique kind of experience that does a great job of combining the strategy and community management of a city builder or village sim with the combat and action of a third-person shooter. It's not without glitches and bugs, but it's also still receiving active patches and free content updates 4 years after release, has no microtransactions, and no nickel-and-diming DLCs. 

[b]For context:[/b] I'm playing on PC (obviously) on a fairly mid-grade machine. It's still on Windows 8.1, ffs. The good news is that the game runs fine even on this derelict. 

[h1]What's it about?[/h1]
You control as small community of survivors struggling to survive and thrive in the zombie apocalypse. A playthrough starts with 3 survivors of your choosing - randomly generated or chosen from your 'legacy pool' of characters saved from previous playthroughs - and you build up the size of your community as you progress. You'll pick a map, move your survivors into in a small starter base, and begin the process of building up your community: scavenging resources, fighting off nearby undead threats, allying or recruiting other survivors, reclaiming territory from the zombies and gradually growing your community and becoming more powerful as a result. 

To do so, you'll establish outposts to help clear unexplored territory, meet other communities to assist and trade, acquire new weapons and important supplies through scavenging or trading, build new facilities in your base, level up and specialize your survivors' skills, elect leaders and unlock special buildings, recruit and train new members to give you additional benefits and abilities, restore and upgrade vehicles to joyride your way through the apocalypse, and more. 

Winning a game typically means finishing a Leader questline to complete their "legacy," which means unlocking a permanent bonus that you can pick to use in future playthroughs. You can then select survivors from your community to add to your legacy pool, and then choose those same hardened veterans (and all their gear and inventory!) and start a new game with them. You can also migrate your community to a whole new region, moving to a new map with everything you accrued on your current one so you can start plundering all over again. 

The persistent legacy bonuses and survivors make for a ton of cool replayability where you're making permanent gains across every playthrough - finding rare items, discovering crucial survivor skills, and unlocking game-changing leader boons that you are permanently available for every subsequent playthrough.

[h1]Pros & Cons[/h1]

[b]THE PROS:[/b]
[list]
[*]That balance of strategy + action is addicting and great fun. The two layers compliment and drive one another; your strategic gains improve your combat capabilities and your combat prowess helps accomplish your strategic goals. 

[*]Configurable difficulty means you can customize your experience to your preferences. Make the combat deadly serious but minimize the community management aspects, or vice-versa. 

[*]The "just one more thing..." feeling is real. It's one of those games that facilitates that sense of having of plans within plans - immediate goals for individual survivors and bigger efforts that take longer, where you're always making progress toward something. 

[*]The stakes are high. You can lose survivors and whole communities if you aren't careful, and the near-death escapes make for the best stories. That sandbox aspect of the game makes for great emergent moments. Or, if you prefer a more chill zombie apocalypse, dial it down to Green Zone and have a relaxing blast. 

[*]You have myriad ways to deal with the challenges before you, especially where your community is concerned. There's a versatile, puzzle-like quality (in a good way!) to the process of optimizing your resources, facilities, survivor needs and more.  

[*]The combination of maps, difficulty levels, legacy boons, leader types, bases, facilities, and randomly-generated survivors means you'll never play the same game twice. With the upcoming (late 2022?) update to enable direct recruitment from your legacy survivor pool, "forever communities" will finally be a reality. 

[*]The power curve is palpable and feels great. You start out vulnerable, with just three people scraping together whatever they can to make it to the next sunrise, and by the end of a playthrough you're smashing through shambling hordes in an armored vehicle that bristles with welded spikes - straight out of Mad Max - while taking down the big guys with .50 cal anti-materiel rifles, C4, assault weapons, etc. You're cowering scared in a dirty garage at the outset, and by the end you've reclaimed a little corner of civilization from the undead horde and are on your way to rebuilding the society that crumbled when the outbreak began. 

[*]Multiple game modes mean you can play the sandbox main game, the story-driven Heartland, or the horde mode Daybreak, depending what you're in the mood for. (Incidentally, those two name game modes were free updates. Undead Labs knows how to treat their fans.)
[/list]

[b]THE CONS:[/b]
[list]
[*]Especially in the early game, it can feel "naggy" with lots of mission prompts popping up frequently and when you're new, it's not always clear what you can ignore or skip. (Which is most of them.)

[*]The game does feel unnecessarily glitchy at times - not in the sense that you crash or freeze constantly, but that the ongoing updates sometimes fix bugs in one area but introduce them in another. 

[*]Optimization could be better - I still get some pop-in textures and landscape assets sometimes, and some of the spawns can get annoying if they appear right in front of you when you're driving at high speed.    

[*]Some of the powerful survivor types (mercenaries from a paramilitary org called Red Talon) and specialized facilities are locked behind the Daybreak horde mode, which can be fun or painful depending on your tastes. Fortunately for PC players, there's a Community Editor mod to circumvent that requirement if you'd like.
[/list]

All in all, [b]highly recommended.[/b] Especially if you like action/strategy combinations, have a hankering for the zombie apocalypse, or just enjoy building and managing a community while staving off external threats.

I was hesitant when my friend asked me to get this game but after playing in his survivor community, creating my own, and finishing my first story, I'm glad he got me playing. The short of it is: if you're looking for a fun solo or co-op open world zombie game, this is one to consider. Read below to get an idea of the game.

State of Decay 2 in so many words is a zombie survival, third person combat game. It features a huge arsenal of recognizable firearms and melee weapons such as the Glock 17 9mm and Crowbar but also had unexpected things the more savvy would recognize such as KSG shotgun or APC9 submachinegun.

I had a few issues with the game in the form of performance. Often when the game cloud-saves, it would freeze my screen for a moment and this was bad for a game like this where zombies are charging me. Gameplay-wise, zombies could occasionally counter my attempts at takedowns with ridiculous reaction speed (I.E. takedown starts and fails because the zombie instantly changes direction to face me) that would cause me to take damage. Some game elements are unclear. When I started, I was unaware that completing a community's story would end that community and they were lost forever. This was luckily changed recently but it still forces you to move to a new area. Weird choices but overall a great experience.

The game caters to a wide array of playstyles and skill levels. You can independently choose how difficult combat is like how much damage zombies dish out and take, how generous or rare loot can be, and how difficult or easy it is to run your survivor community. (I play on Lethal zombies, Green map, and Green community, so combat is always a challenge but the rewards are also great and my community isn't too hard to run for me.)

The game world feels full of stuff to do. You assign a leader to your group and, depending on the character, they can become a type of leader and that dictates the sort of attitude your community has to the world. This is very customizable, too, because even though you are given the choice of two characters who then get two more in the tutorial, you can completely trade out anyone. Often you'll be visited by someone wanting to join your community and you can say yes or no. You can dress up your survivors, give them weapons, you can even recruit one to follow you if you're lonely and they have unlimited ammo as an AI. You could be driving on a supply run and get a call on the radio to go help a neighbor but you don't HAVE to, though they might die forever or turn into a hostile group. Bandits might move into town.

One of the big gameplay elements is how you layout your home. Where you make your home matters and there are different ways to lay it out based on what you need and want. You might not need to find a power source because your home has power built-in.

The big core combat challenge is clearing the "Blood Plague" from the area. Several spots on the map will be super dangerous to go to because blood plague kills quickly and makes zombies stronger. It's a decent challenge and incredibly cinematic the way it plays out clearing them. Oh and also this game does perma-death so if you lose a character, they are gone and that adds to the tension greatly. On Lethal combat difficulty, I was always cautious but it never felt like I died instantly. This is a play smarter not harder game.

Give it a try and if it's on sale, maybe bring some friends.

State of Decay 1 is an excellent game and State of Decay 2 improves on pretty much everything. However if you are a completionist be aware it's got some hard and very grindy achievements.

This review assumes you are familiar with SoD1. If not I suggest you read my SoD1 review and consider playing that game first. It's well worth your time but after playing the 2nd it may seem a little lacking.

SoD2 - the graphics are better, there are now 6 maps to choose from and there are more facilities, vehicles and weapons. You can customise your character's skills more and even change their clothing. Missions are more varied and enclaves play a much bigger part. There is also multi player but I only sampled that briefly for a couple of achievements.

Also some of the annoying features in SoD1 have been removed. Time no longer continues when you exit the game and you are no longer bombarded with notifications every 30 seconds. Morale is now community based so no more having to constantly swap and play with every survivor to keep their morale up. Survivors no longer go missing from base.

The not so improved is infestations can be a pain to fully clear and then there is the constant darkness. A day lasts 90 minutes of which only 30 minutes is daylight. Fortunately there is a longer daylight mod you can use.

The base game has 5 difficulty settings. Green, Standard, Dread, Nightmare and Lethal. The objective is to destroy Plague Hearts and then there are 4 story arcs where you select either a Builder, Trader, Sheriff or Warlord as your leader. There are achievements for completing at least 1 story arc in Nightmare and the other 3 in Dread.

To make things easier you can start a game on say Standard and once you've built up your skills and gear then switch to nightmare. The story will reset but you'll be in a much stronger position to deal with it. You don't need to complete the game in Lethal but there are some achievements where you have to play in Lethal to get them.

One of the grind achievements is to survive until day 100 in Dread. This isn't difficult but as I said earlier, a day lasts 90 minutes so this is going to take you 150 hours. I built up a self sustaining base with a Haven Device (auto kills any zombie that gets close) then left the game running in the background.

Like SoD1 all the DLC is included. The 1st main DLC is Daybreak which has you and up to 3 other players defending against waves of zombies. If you are aiming for 100% you need to beat wave 5 solo and wave 7 (can be co-op) a number of times. You also need to beat a total of 343 waves which is another grind achievement.

Wave 5 solo is hard. I kept beating wave 3 until I unlock the Cleo Shotgun and Rocket Pods which helped enormously. To beat wave 7 I highly recommend you do this with a partner, it is so much easier. Once you've unlock all wave 7 rewards it's then more efficient to just keep beating waves 1 and 2 until you've completed 343 waves.

Another thing to note, it's worth playing Daybreak before or along side the main game because some of the rewards can be used in the main game and some are required for achievements.

The other main DLC is Heartland where you return to Trumbull Valley, the original map from SoD1. This includes a larger campaign where you are now up against Plague Walls which are a stronger version of a Plague Heart. There are achievements for recruiting various survivors and you'll need at least one and a half playthroughs to get them all. You also need to complete the game solo and with a partner. For the with partner you can simply join a game just before the last mission.

To sum things up, SoD2 is excellent. Daybreak is ok but those 343 waves are painful and Heartland is more of the same with a better story.

First I would like to start with what is great about this game even though I do have to give it an overall down thumb, if it could be done with stars I would give it a 2 out of 5.
The Great:
It truly is an open world sandbox zombie survival that lets you play the game they way you wish to play it, you can play as an aggressive warlord, lawful sheriff, a trader who makes friends, a builder, or anything in-between to what suites you the best.
The different options in difficulty let you play as hard or easy as you want giving everyone from casual gamers to hardcore survival gamers something to look forward to.

Secondly, The Good

The actions you do in the game have effects that can hurt your relations with different groups, though all the time sometimes gifts that get dropped as rewards like supply sacks when picked up get counted as "theft" and will turn a group hostile to you.
The missions given to you by your own survivors and enclaves vary some, but after a while it begins to feel like the same type of missions over and over again, get supplies, guard while I search, clear nests, ect...
The amount of zombies in the game itself is great, sometimes there are comforting luls in the chaos allowing you to look around and enjoy the scenery, but expect it to be destroyed by a random home siege even if your noise production is extremely low, or some random zombies that somehow spawned inside of the temporary "safezone" you created after searching and clearing a building.
The Meh

Don't expect the AI you bring along with you to dodge explosives you throw, or help you kill zombies, or hostile humans, or be anything other than a pack mule. I understand programming them to not be hyper aggressive so they don't start unneeded fights, but they will just stand there and watch you die sometimes. They will also leave the gates to your base open, and they WILL NOT close if an AI opened it.

Removed features, if you are like me you ran the first game into the ground playing it, there are 2 features which I personally loved that are now gone, hiding in bushes does nothing, and you can no longer board windows up. Instead of the devs improving these features to give them more of a highlight, like giving your base window upgrades can reduce noise via creating sound barriers, and bushes being able to be used to sneak up on infected easier, so people would use them more often than in the first game, they opted to be a little lazy and just remove it.

Your characters animations, inputs, and other animations feel really clunky and forced, you can get combat locked onto a zombie thats on the ground 2 feet away instead of the zombie your camera is pointed toward i.e probably that screamer thats summoning some more friends while you swing aimlessly at the air. 

Fuel and vehical repair, even with a 30% reduction in fuel usage via special buildings at your base, expect to have to always carry 2 extra tanks with you, driving 1km will run your fuel 3/4 the way down on most cases, and unless your hitting every zombie with your door, or dodging them like an indie game, your vehical will be run down by the end of your trips.

Zombie spawn patterns, sometimes if feels a little odd that in the middle of a city you can run into maybe 20-30 zombies while clearing out whole blocks, while running on the country side you will run into consistent hordes of about 15-20 so maybe a little balancing needs to be done there.

The Really Bad
Bugs, there are plenty of bugs in the game that mess with you, from clipping into the ground, to vehicals flying off for an adventure, there is a radio command to unstick you, but after being out for so long more of these bugs should have been squashed considering online through nexus modding community you can find some that have been created just to squash bugs. If modders who make no money can fix the bugs in your game, you can to end of story.

If there is a group fight going on between you and other survivors, unless you learn the dodging mechanic, that the game doesn't tell you in the basic tutorial it's C by the way, expect to be stun locked by an AI perma swinging that tiny axe they all carry. The game first informed me of the dodging mechanic 6-hrs into the game. Also, if you are melee fighting survivors expect to have to knock them down 3 or 4 times before they die due to not being able to execute them, or if you are supposed to be able to I have never had that option.

If there is a bunch of zombies and survivors fighting, you will get animation run locked if you just try to swing your weapon, where you will run in place for anywhere from 3-5 seconds letting zombies hit you for free.

Special Infected, for these zombies to be special there shouldn't be as many of them spawning as there are, in some cases you might get all of them spawning on top of each other meaning you basically cannot go to an area because killing them all might be just to much of a pain for newer players.

AI enclaves have a habit of spawning on-top of zombie nests, meaning when you visit you could end up potentially having to fight infected and hostile survivors at the same time.

The AI across the board is mediocre at best, and dreadful to deal with at worst, survivors you bring along are normally just cannon fodder or pack mules, they get stuck on doors, doorways, perma jumping in and out of windows/walls, running in infinite circles, or sometimes even shooting you even when allied or friendly. 
UPDATE: Since the AI update I have only played the game an extra few hours just to test out what was changed on them, they don't randomly jump over walls/through windows anymore or attack a heart when you're near it if you're sneaking which is really nice. BUT they now have this weird tendency to stare at the sky with their gun pointed to it, and now they don't attack back when zombies are hitting them they just kind of run around them until they die or you kill the zombies hitting them. They will also randomly walk outside the walls of your base and get merced by zombies for a bit before the other AI react to help or you go help them as well. So i still recommend just leaving them in base to hoard the good hero stats you like but don't stay to long to them now randomly leaving base and taking a bunch of damage for zero reason.

Supply moving is a hassle, if you have a car full of stuff that you want to transport parked in a parking spot, expect to make a bunch of trips in and out of your car even with an option exisiting allowing you to move supplies into your car, but not out of your car into the stockpile.
Edit: The Game Will show you eventually that T will auto move stuff from your car to storage, took 20 hours for that tool tip to show.

Your Backpack alone will most likely always weigh more than what you're actually carrying inside it, a large pack will weigh 16 pounds alone, so unless you have the backpacking cardio skill, for most of your characters it will be useless due to the complete drain on your stamina.

Hearts effects: The effects of destroying hearts do not seem to be as much as really needed, it would be more interesting as the more hearts your destroyed the less special infected spawn and larger groups spawned in the wild, but instead they more focused around the areas closer to the hearts giving the game some more sense of destroying the hearts being beneficial in some areas where there is no heart present but more disastrous in area where they are present still.

Thank you to all who read all the way through this long review/post, some of the information is purely personal preference, while other stuff is generic that will probably bother you as well at some point.

State of Decay 2 is an open world survival game where the player takes charge of a small community of survivors in the zombie apocalypse.

I played the original game several years ago, and I remember thinking it was mostly good while having a few minor bugs. The sequel has very similar gameplay mechanics and thankfully is a more polished experience.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

•	Improve your base by building various rooms including basics like a barracks where your characters can rest and a medical tent to heal wounds, and more advanced facilities like the workshop where you can craft items, and the shooting range and fighting gym to upgrade your characters’ skills.

•	Scavenge abandoned buildings for supplies including food, medicine, ammo, building materials, and fuel. You can also create outposts that provide regular deliveries to your base.

•	Grow your community by recruiting new characters. The player can control any character in your group, and you can travel with an AI controlled companion who will assist in combat, and help you carry more stuff. If you like to customise your characters’ appearance, there are lots of cosmetic items to choose from.

•	Use a wide variety of blunt and bladed melee weapons, several guns including pistol, assault rifle, smg, shotgun and crossbow, and a few different grenade types. You can also sneak up behind zombies for stealth kills, and get road kills while you drive around town.

•	As well as regular zombies there are specials like the bloater, screamer, feral and juggernaut (all similar to Left 4 Dead’s special infected). Meanwhile, some buildings have been taken over by plague hearts, which are glowing masses of flesh that create plague zombies, whose attacks can infect your characters.

•	Infected characters can be cured if you act quickly enough, but if they become fully infected, or if someone loses all health, they’ll die permanently.

•	There are two story campaigns which took me a combined 23 hours to complete. Story quests involve helping other groups of survivors who are incapable of doing anything for themselves, to clear zombie infested buildings, gather supplies, find special items, or defend their base against Human bandits. There’s also a basic horde mode where you have to defend a technician from waves of zombies.

•	Controls work great with mouse and keyboard. I had some framerate issues during the first couple of hours, but after playing around with some graphics settings it seems fine now.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

State of Decay 2 is mostly very enjoyable to play. It gives me the feeling of managing a Walking Dead style community (but with less sitting around listening to Carol being miserable). I recommend buying at full price or a small sale.

I played the first one over a thousand hours on multiple platforms (PC and console).  So I might be a bit biased, or you might be just like me, you decide.  But, this is one of my favorite series of all time.  It is not an objectively good series.  It is deeply flawed in design and execution and not for everyone.  But despite it being rough around the edges, I love it to death.  Its ambitious, original/different, and the concept just sucks me in.  I don't hesitate to buy it full price and hope they make these forever.

I'm going to keep it short for those who haven't played it.  Its an open world game where you find, customize survivors and build out their specialties.  Is the doctor going to have improved stealth or improved carrying capacity for example.  Decide their weapons.  Should this guy carry a loud and long range bolt action with 7.62 ammo, a lightweight .22 pistol, or a short ranged auto in 9mm?  A crowbar, metal bat, or machete?  There is a degree of luck with personality and traits and sometimes you stumble across people who are awesome, useless (who you can proceed to exile), and sometimes people who are deceivingly awesome, but end up being a hassle.  Characters are thrown at you dynamically and its never the same each playthrough.  Choose between the woman who was a former cop or the guy who was a mechanic.  Either brings a certain skill to your base.  You recruit them, only to find out they are annoying your other survivors (-morale) and eat double rations.

Next, you find and collect resources and customize your base.  After you find a good spot to settle, there is a limited number of indoor/outdoor small/large spaces and you have to make decisions on what to build.  A solar panel for electricity or an autoshop to turn your vehicles into mad max monster machines for example.  The game then proceeds to throw missions and story at you, but really that's not the highlight of the game.  The game, in my opinion, is more about the team you build, the skills you have, the base facilities that compliment them, the loot you find, rinse and repeat.

If you played the first, there has been equal steps forward and equal steps back in my opinion.  It is still very much the same look and feel which is a good thing.  The campaign story mode is open world and once complete, you can replay one of the 4 maps allowing the surviving characters, items, and bonuses to carry over in new game plus.  You can save up to 50 of your survivors, but choose only 3 to start a new map.  Its like they took the campaign of story mode and combined it with aspects of Breakdown to create an improved campaign mode.  I personally like it much better than the first.  

There's a lot of little improvements too... they removed annoying survey missions, added sieges similar to Lifeline where your base gets attacked by waves of zombies actually putting your defenses/characters to the test, plague hearts are like infestions 2.0, more character passives like +beds +morale and others, the ability to mod and customize bases (space heaters, ammo presses, additional storage, etc), some nice new traders, weapons, abilities, and some more.  

And some negatives... outposts are not safe and landmine hordes, survivor pop limit of 9ish (soft cap), vehicles need micromanaged repairs and fuel, zombie spawns can be cheap and persist on long playtimes (they keep throwing more and more at you and you can ignore it, but if you exit the game and restart, things go back to normal), missions are still tedious and repetitive, they have you driving all over the map, they throw way too many missions at you at once and they expire too quickly, AI is still kinda stupid and get themselves in trouble and/or ignore you needing assistance, and even smaller annoyances similar to the first like getting stuck on curbs and entering a vehicle instead of stomping a zombie head because they both use the same button.

Overall though its an improvement over the first and a great game in the series.  I'm already looking to 3 and hope they don't change the formula too much.  This is not your AAA game/story on rails and cinematics.  This is an open world zombie sandbox with an indie vibe.  If you were a fan of the first, you'll enjoy this.  But I'm also not seeing it convert many people who didn't like the first one.

Moreso, however, I am just disappointed. We would have spent so much time on this game. Now we'll be asking for refunds.

Developers, please consider a true cooperative mode. In the interim, fix the one that's already there. And more importantly? Finish a game before you charge people for it. I'm not your QA employee, I'm a paying customer. Or, well, I was one. Undead Labs has a lot of work ahead to make the experience more generally enjoyable for its fans, and I have little confidence they have any intention of doing it. The fixes are simple on the surface, but almost certainly systemic. As identified by the broader community, what we need to see is:

> OPTIONS (high priority)

--- Toggle whether a joining player can control community members, and/or affect its management.

> FIXES (emergency)
--- Technical issues abound. This game has been out for a year. It shouldn't still be hard crashing, freezing, or otherwise becoming unplayable so frequently that half the community is regularly experiencing it.

> IMPROVEMENTS (long-term)
--- AI pathing
--- Weather
--- UI Design
--- Traits, personalities, etc

A true cooperative experience is [i]so close[/i] that it is frankly shocking how hard UL and Microsoft dropped the proverbial ball. This is fixable. It should have already been done. Now we just wait to see how much they care about their community.

[b] Maps [/b]
     They look absolutely amazing. Each one of them is unique and with different difficulty. Pros and cons. If you are beginner, I´d say the [u] Meagher Valley [/u] is the best one. It´s area with farmland, small neighbourhoods, enough ressources and excelent bases. My favourite one was Squelones Brewing Company - you can actually brew your booze and trade that for influence points - which can get you really useful upgrades for your base, guns, and other stuff you need. 

Next one is [u] Cascade Hills [/u]
     Its an okay map, with a lot of wrecked vehicles, connected buildings and two rivers going through the country, but i found myself spending too much time only on the west side of the map due to inbalance of ressources. 

[u] Drucker County [/u] 
     You can tell the army presence was much greater than in other maps, you can find many blockades, evacuation centers. Its by far the hardest map for me. The hills, cliffs, huge rocks, make it hard to travel and i cant even count how many times i flipped my car over one. (thanks to devs for having the "flip the car" option in game lol)

[u] Providence Ridge [/u]
     Newest map SoD2 has to offer. You will start in a small outpost uphill with few buildings nearby and city lurking just as close. Giving me some logging town  vibes with lumberjack statue and surrounding feels like somewhere in the north of the USA. Great starting map. 

If you're not happy with current map, you can simply upgrade radio station and choose option to move to different map. 

[b] Radio [/b]
     Use it as much as you can. You can call for ressources, find another survivors, traders, or you can call for help. That will search another player who are willing to help you. Or you can volunteer and help someone. Theres also stuck command, which says more about the state of the game than you think - its for the moments you find yourself stuck in texture/unable to move/vehicles get stuck.

[b] Bases [/b]
     You will come across facilities connected to each other with wire fences around them - that right there could be your new home. 

     Facilities i mentioned are different in each base. For example base located in Providence Ridge has already built-in Fuel Storage and Auto shop that teaches Mechanics skill, and then theres Barricaded Strop Mall in Drucker County with built-in gym and Urgent Care to keep your survivors healthy and happy. 

     But beware, the more you build at once, the more noise you make. It can end up with Zeds surrounding your base. so keep the noise down.
Each base also has open slots. It depends only on your needs to decide, what to build there.

     You can also claim outpost. I recommend not to claim outpost nearby your base. If you find yourself out in the middle of nowhere its great to have outpost spread over the whole country, because it provides safe place and locker so you can drop off what you dont need atm or take precious meds. Also each outpost provides differend bonus for you. Some will give you daily fuel, meds, food, some coffee which means higher morale for your community. 

     Speaking of morale, dont ignore it. People will fight, be upset over not enough food/meds, not enough beds if theres too many survivors. Pay attention to this, because [b] they can leave [/b] .

Now, with release on Steam/Epic the game got neat upgrades such as Bounties which can get you some nice guns, clothes and facility mods. Big thumbs up. 

[b] Audio experience [/b]
is also so much better, new music, sound effects. No wonder when the soundtrack is from Jesper Kyd. He has composed soundtracks for the Hitman series, Assassin's Creed series, Borderlands series, Darksiders II etc. 

      All together the feeling of playing/moving around feels much nicer than it did before. But as I read through the patch notes i have to laugh when i see " We fixed dozens of mission and gameplay bugs to ensure a better experience for all players." Excuse me what? 

[b] Adding new, not fixing the old  [/b]
      Here comes my b1tchy me. Theres dozens (bugs) of them still left. One would think that two years of data from players and updates would fix the major bugs that just kept breaking the game. 

     But multiplayer experience is as bad as it was two years ago and that is just sad. Invisible Zeds, car being shot across the map, Zeds glitching in the texture not being able to kill them/clear area/finish missions. And those endless disconnects... But when all you do is invite your friends over and over again because game kicks them out at the most stupid moment.. it becomes tiring.

     I dont give up. Maybe the fact that its finally on Steam will make you fix at least some of those flaws, because more people can finally voice their opinion. Also I really wish they'd bring back the ability to barricade windows. Like in the first SOD, Its way easy for Zeds to get inside your base. 

     The fact you need Xbox Live account  to be able to play this game also feels a bit like a waste of time.

And here we are. 
I wish there would be [b] "Meh I guess?" [/b] botton, because thats how I feel about it right now. Yes and No. More of a Yes. To put it bluntly, this game feels like the most real zombie apocalypse game I have ever played. Sure, sometimes the zombies spawn inside of rocks and my car flips upside down. But the characters and situations are so realistic. I had my first survivor die, and I felt actual remorse. I thought what could I had done different even though I had never played her, only spoke to her. I got sad as I drove back to my base and realized I'd have to face her partner who was alive when she wasn't. I haven't played a game this real in some time, and I would happily recommend it. Am I playing on the easiest setting? Yes. Will I up it? No.

State of Decay 2 while is initially pretty engaging eventually runs into mediocrity thanks to the raw repetition of things  but it'll take you quite awhile to get to that point. State of Decay 2 on the right difficulty will leave you with dramatic scrambles to deal with hordes of zombies or special zombies if you manage things poorly or do not bring the needed supplies to deal with it and absolute success with reasonable planning and patience. It's a really solid zombie open world shooter if you're into that thing.

The biggest standout feature is the community system, which is new as well as having multiple maps to play on. The character generation is fairly big with different survivors having different sets of skills that they can bring to your base, meaning that they aren't divorced completely from your base like they kinda were in the first SOD. Each base has it's ups and downs, even if it seems like a straight upgrade. Some bigger bases are just frankly utterly terrible for dispatching hordes and juggernauts, they'll flood in and everything turns into a bloodbath. The key is picking the one that has many good spots for survivors to dispatch zombies while having key faculties that help manage your community. The upgrades aren't as essential as they seem, some quests and outposts you can setup in the openworld provide for the spaces in your base development you cannot fill. It's just way way way way better than the original State of Decay, which was a very annoying system to deal with. 

Another big part is the dynamic nature of the game as a sandbox. Survivors are generated randomly, whole other communities are randomly generated too. The game invites you to make your own player driven stories through those interactions often finally peaking with a designated leader and their ultimate goal for the community. This is essentially your endgame. It's a great way of pacing the game out a little and you get bonuses for completing a "community" every time you do this. Then you can take survivors from your current playthrough and save them for future playthroughs, so if you like that mechanic guy who you saved from a juggernaut and he learnt to build all your badass cars for you and you want him to come along for another ride? You can totally do that. It's pretty flexible and adds a level of meta progression that grows stronger with you being invested emotionally and gameplay wise. It's generally a pretty fun system.

The problems with this system is repetition, you will start to see the same sort of events happen over and over around your third playthrough. The community's overall goal and that questline of sorts rarely changes. It always sorta rolls out the same way which doesn't hurt too bad because most of the time your community progression is built towards making the area you are in safer from plague hearts (essentially red zombie disease) first and foremost. Be it through allying yourself with other communities and trading for supplies or them directly assisting with dispatching them. 

The moment to moment gameplay isn't spectacular, especially as other third person shooters go but it's serviceable. There are a looooot of guns. A lot of weapons. There is a lot of loot to collect and find. If you like grabbing everything in a building that isn't nailed down, this might be your game. Zombies are fairly intense to fight as well, they aren't pushovers especially on your own. If you're on a weak character and the difficulty is high, watch your ass because it won't take much to kill you. If a feral shows up and you're low on health? Your character is dead. The game appreciates stealth chiefly of all but it has the drawback of being a slow way to play the game and frankly kinda boring even if it's a really strong way to play. Go in guns blazing, slashing everything. It's a zombie game after alll! 

A short piece of coop, it's a really flawed unfun system that i am surprised is this halfbaked. It's not good. I hope to see maybe coop communities (maybe set it up similar to stardew valley?) in a third game out of Undead Labs because the sheer amount that you are locked out of doing as a coop partner is aloooooot. It's really not great. Don't get this as a coop game.

I think there is a lot here in State of Decay 2 to enjoy, not for as long as other games but it's an immensely fun journey if you're the right person for it. The foundation here is a lot stronger than SOD1 and i can see this evolving into something really awesome if they nailed out the game's design issues. Think 7 Days to Die but you're managing a whole group of survivors, your friends included. That would be insanely awesome. Undead Labs has put a lot of effort into the post-release content and understanding what people want from this game. I can't recommend this game if you're obviously lukewarm on the genre or open world games in general but if you are then you're gonna have fun for at least 10-30 hours. That's a good sell for a game pass game.

[list]
[*]Major improvement from the first game - but, it's still the same base mechanics. 
[*]The character customization has been improved. It's more like an RPG in that sense now. And they've added several hundreds of new available traits, quirks, skills, community skills, and hero bonuses.
[*]Legacy boons, goals, and missions. Completing a playthrough with a certain leader on a certain difficulty permanently unlocks really powerful legacy boons that you can take with you on the next playthrough. 
[*]A lot of new types of facilities for your base, tons of new items, consumables, weapons, cars, upgrades, textbooks to learn skills, etc.
[*]New types of special infected.
[*]New and/or improved mechanics like sieges, Blood Plagues, LegacyBoons, Bounty Hunter, etc.
[*]5 maps to choose from. After you've completed one, you can save 3 survivors from that playthrough and reuse them in the next one.
[*]No story whatsoever. The game just assumes that you've played the first one. Not that it's really needed but if you are to understand the small remarks storywise, it requires you to have played and remembered the story of the first game.
[*]Multiplayer. This was the most requested feature and if played with the right people, is really fun. Bear in mind that MP is based on the host and that person decides where you go, which missions you'll do, control its base, buildings, etc. You can only join with a character from your game and the items that the character has on him. Containers are color-coded in MP and you can only open 'your' containers. And there are no anti-cheat measures in MP. Someone can join with a simple trainer active and stop the time, edit health, spawn in hordes, have unlimited ammo, gasoline, etc. Can really be a deal-breaker. 
[*]Hero bonuses and leaders available after your character has done good deeds enough. Different leaders have different endings and different specializations and structures for your base.
[*]New unique threats, Blood Plague, Plague Hearts, and Plague Walls.
[*]Clothing and customization of characters are now a thing. You'll need to find the clothes for them to be permanently added. Or get them from the Bounty Hunter if you're fast enough before time runs out and those opportunities are gone forever.
[*]Unique mode, Daybreak. You'll defend a small outpost against several waves of zombies while playing as Red Talon Operators/Soldiers, either in SP or MP. For doing this, you'll gain Prestige which can be used in the regular game mode to hire Red Talon contractors and buy unique facilities for your base. These are extremely overpowered but on the other hand very, very expensive to get.
[*]Revisit Trumbull Valley from the first game in the Heartland DLC. It's now 1/4 smaller but has an incredible storyline where you'll learn more about the Blood Plague, the virus's origins, and how to potentially destroy it.
[*]2 other DLC's, Doomsday and Independence Pack. Both add vehicles, weapons, and items, obtained by radio calls as supply drops. There are also some pre-order bonus packs, which can no longer be obtained unless you mod the game or download a trainer/tool for it. 
[*]Active modding community.
[/list]

The only thing it's lacking is really major content, after you have finished all the community legacy's you're not really left with anything to do aside from playing the harder difficulties or play Daybreak and Heartland. But that'll take a while, especially now with the fairly new difficulty level, Lethal Zone. Dark Souls ain't nothing compared to SOD2's Lethal Zone.

Edit: After more hours of playing, I want to give a little longer review on State Of Decay 2.

The core of the game is something really amazing and truly unique. I've always wanted a zombie survival game with management elements and the only similar game close to that experience was 7 Days to Die which is also an amazing game.

Unfortunately, the game has a lot of flaws and I'm going to list the ones I know about below.

1. The game is filled with bugs and glitches!
I can't tell you about how many the times I was stuck in an object or my car getting stuck in terrain or actions not working as intended.
While these bugs won't hurt you if you're playing on Normal Zone, they will definitely get your characters killed on harder difficulties.

2. The multiplayer is designed in the worst possible way!
Similar to games like Dark Souls, you can't have shared community with a friend. Instead, a friend can join your session with their own community to assist you in your game. Of course, the party members will have progression on their characters, but their base will stay untouched unless they play on their own game as well. The party members can't even edit their base while they're on someone else's game which really sucks
The game also limits the party members to the host's vicinity which means you can't get too far away from the host.

3. The AI is kind of dumb!
Don't get me wrong, because they've been greatly improved over time but they're still not fully compatible! Survivors running in a circle or doing nothing, followers just standing still while you're fighting a horde and zombies standing in one place and not doing anything despite spotting you and a lot more!

4. Lack of story options and connection with survivors!
I get that this is not an RPG game and the survivors are generated randomly, but throughout the game, there were points I wish I had different options when interacting with other survivors.
Also, the survivors in this game are less of a survivor and more of a resource! There are so many times I've lost a member of my community or exiled them without caring at all!

Overall, I really enjoyed the game and would recommend it to casual gamers and survival fans. The game WILL annoy you if you get easily frustrated so be wary. I have enjoyed all the time I've put into this game and you can bet I'll put even more hours!
