TLDR: A unique zombie survival game that has so much potential that is wasted by easily fixable issues.

So State of Decay 2 is another zombie survival game. But instead of beating trees and collecting rocks to build a spaceship you have to run through abandoned buildings in search for food, weapons and medicine. In the harsh world of State of decay 2 not everybody is supposed to survive. You will have to make tough choices to keep your community alive.

I am really sorry to give this game a negative review because the game itself is really really good but Undead Labs REALLY has to work on quality assurance.

Many of the things that annoyed me were my own fault in the end because i did not understand certain game mechanics (so expect to git gud). But there are just so much frustrating and especially unecesserary problems.

Heavy issues:
- One of your survivors has a gun on him that you really need to get medicine. So you select him. But what is that? If you select him now his personal quest will start and you are not allowed to change the character again or the quest will dissappear(and maybe come back, or maybe not). This quest would give you ammunition that you also need right after medicine. So now you are stuck with the personal quest. Why cant you just start the personal quests by clicking on the questlog after you have selected the required character?!?!?! I absolutely dont get this restriction.
- The Follower AI is one of the worst i have ever seen. Sometimes you try to escape from a zombie horde with your car BUT NO your buddy got stuck in a door or decided to fight the horde all by his own. There should be commands like "Come to me" which aborts everything the NPC does so he runs to you. Sometimes they just stand there while you are being eaten by a zombie.
- So many quality of life things. One of your members has the blood plague so you put him in the infirmary. Now you have to remove the member again if you want to access his inventory. This includes the community management screen which is a total mess. If you want a specific member to follow you, you have to search for them in the entire base. Easy when you only have 3 members. Annoying when you have a base of 15 people. This is something that could be integrated so easily into the "Community" screen. Or when you know that one of the people has a certain weapon on them but you dont remember who. So you have to search and check every member again. Why not just implement an inventory screen in the community screen?!?!?!?
- Like in every video game you are once again the only being that can get shit done. So you are fighting 2 juggernauts, two bloodplague hordes and a plague heart at the moment? Well the enclaves dont care. They are like little children that dont understand they are not the center of the universe and expect you to drop everything right now and go to them. YES i know you are not supposed to be everyones darling but it is still annoying that you cant even explain to them that you were fighting for your fucking life and therefore couldnt help them at the moment.
- There should be "starting areas" at least regarding the juggernaut. The bloodplague-juggernaut is the most dangerous zombie in the game and must be hard of course, especially on nightmare. But when they spawn next to your base at the beginning there is just nothing you can do and he will infect everybody he did not kill, if not wipe your whole community. This is especially an issue that would have make me stop playing if i didnt learn about a cheesetactic to kill a juggernaut. Otherwise, even in lategame i would have to avoid juggernauts because you have to burn nearly all your ammunition to kill one.
- Zombie spawning rate is really really high, which is fine because this game is about zombie killing and not triggering zombie hordes. But it does not matter if you are in the town center or on a big open field with no buildings in sight, there will be zombies everywhere. This breaks the immersion for me. You can clear buildings that will make a safezone around them (although i often see zombies in them anyway) but those last just for a day or so. And there is just no time to clear them. I even had moments when i was fighting a plague heart and a horde with 2 juggernauts suddenly appeared that were definetaley not nearby before.
- Lategame gets very repetetive. When you cleaned out all plague hearts all you can do is make your legacy or move to another map and clean all plague hearts again.

Minor Issues:
- Bugs
- Bad explanation of gamemechanics and skills. The tutorial explains the essential mechanics of course. But many important mechanics are not mentioned. Like killing zombies with your cardoor or the rear avoids cardamage. Or when you look at the skills of a potential recruit but when you hover of the skills the explanation does not appear(only when you own that character).

I could go on about the stuff that annoys me so much but could be fixed so easily and should be expected in a Juggernaut-Edition after 2 years of feedback. Thats why i have to give a negative review unfortunately.

Beneath all this unnecessary frustrating problems is a really good zombie game. One of the best zombiesetting i have played to be honest next to Undying light. The game forces you to make hard choices.
There can be a situation where two of your members got the blood plague but you only have 1 antidode left and not enough resources to make a second one. Because you have no medicine you can neither put one in the infarmy to "park" the character with the blood plague.
So you have to make a decision who lives and who leaves (if you just keep an infected member in the base the blood plague can spread).

Just like in XCOM you feel attached to your characters that survive long enough. Because if a member dies they stay dead. That hurts especially when the person that died was your only doctor and maxed out zombiekiller.

A limited resource storage forces you for a proper resourcemanagement. You think you can just grind a lot of Food and then relax? Well nope. In the beginning you can have 15 food max in your base. All food above that gets lost after time. But your people burn 3-4 food away every day which sounds like plenty of time but be aware that it is not only food. All the storage mechanics applies to medicine, materials, ammo and gas. So you constantly have to weigh which resource has the highest priority right now.

Zombie smashing is fun. Its not the best animations and fightingsystem i have ever seen but hitting or slashing a zombie feels really "meaty". You can suplex them, cut their legs, overthrow, execute, burn, shoot, blow up or just drive your car over a zombie.

The car balancing is ok, although they could be buffed. You can of course run over zombies with a car but that will also damage the car quickly. To avoid car damage you can use the cardoors that will fall off after time too though. Hitting zombies with your rear does not damage the car at all. So in the end you are driving in reverse the whole time which is a bit weird.

Gun balancing is also really sweet. Guns and ammo are rare but not too rare. It makes a big difference if you just shoot mindlessly (and have constantly ammoshortage) or use the weapons just for emergency situtations and use headshots.

In conclusion:
If you are looking for a tough and fun zombie survival game State of Decay 2 is just right. But expect a lot of frustrating moments that you need to endure and could be fixed if undead labs wanted to.

While I always felt magnetized to the original State of Decay for its innovative and relentless design philosophy, its performance, visuals, and controls held it back from being a title I could earnestly enjoy. Undead Labs completely rectify those issues with this sequel and provide the best survival game, and one of the all-around best games, that I've played.

You are tasked with maintaining a community of survivors in one of several large sandboxes, and given no true direct priority beyond getting by from day to day. What makes State of Decay truly unique is that its blend of party management, base-building and third-person exploration co-exist within a reciprocating and complimentary balance, all in real-time. Hordes and infestations increase, supplies fluctuate, and neighboring communities make actions on a minute-to-minute basis, an extremely uncommon and bold mechanic within the open-world genre normally engineered to be as stress-free and empowering as possible.

Speaking of stress, that's all you'll be feeling for most of your run, but in a great way. When any character can easily die at any time, including a siege at home, the pressure to make the right decisions and future-proof your base and members is always on. As such, every battle victory, sweet piece of loot, and teammate becomes all the sweeter to relish in. It's hard not to invest in and become attached to your characters, and there aren't many more true dread-instilling experiences in games than feeling the threat of death encroaching upon one of them. While some folks dislike that characters are broad and generic, I love that this allows me to place a "face" upon each of them within my imagination, and truly tell their stories through the gameplay.

Going along this point, especially refreshing for me was the lack of a focal narrative attempting to structure the experience like there had been within the original. When a game is as systemic and free-form as this, I prefer all the focus to be put upon the spontaneous experiences that arise from that quality, as opposed to having the narrative written for me. I've always sought out free-form sandboxes in the vein of Mount & Blade, and this is essentially the Mount & Blade of zombie sims, both in spirit and overall quality.

The gameplay is utterly compulsive. I've already pulled a couple all-nighters optimizing my base, scouting out good loot and outposts, improving my characters, and building relations with other enclaves. The risk-reward nature of every venture into the world keeps you in a perpetual loop of adrenaline and dopamine. It's truly the moments when you let your guard down at all in State of Decay 2 that you get absolutely destroyed. The one and only death within my first community lay claim to a Navy vet named Knight. I had really grown to dislike this guy over the few hours I'd had him due to how much he'd glitch out, complain, and fight. But then I brought him along on a roadtrip, and he began to open up to me about his first date as a teenager. He was right in the middle of talking about taking her to a movie or some shit, when a bloater I'd totally failed to spot strolled in front of our truck and gassed us out. As we leapt out of the car, two ferals and a horde of blood plaguers began encroaching. I was able to skirt around them just enough to get out of their attention and back into the truck, but Knight got swarmed. They'd surrounded him on a rocky slope, which made it harder to plow over them. As I took desperate maneuvers to try and clear out the freaks, Knight pleaded for help in terrified agony. Just like in the movies, I was seconds too late to save him. The same man who'd authentically pissed me off with his shenanigans, who'd just recently begun winning my respect for his humanity, and who'd been recalling a happier moment in his early life just a minute earlier, now lay on a slab of stone with his head shattered like a grape, and it's all because I'd been too interested in his story to fully focus on the road. It is the closest approximation to real existential dread and the fragility of life that I've encountered in a video game, and it was entirely unscripted. Hilarious and haunting at the same time.

Other strong points: the FANTASTIC soundtrack, the memorably disturbing zombie designs, animations and audio, the humour and personality, and the sick 180-turns you can pull off in cars to send zombies flying.

All-in-all, State of Decay 2 is a must-play for anyone who enjoys simulations, zombies, survival games, and/or memorable open-worlds. This gem will masterfully sate your appetite for all of the above. A new top-10 favourite.

Recommended. After more than 1,000 hours, State of Decay 2 is still one of the best zombie survival sandbox games I’ve played. The real strength is not just fighting zombies, but managing your community, choosing survivors, building a base, balancing resources, developing skills, and deciding who is worth risking on dangerous missions. Every community feels a little different, and the combination of permadeath, random survivors, loot, enclaves, plague hearts, vehicles, and difficulty settings gives the game a huge amount of replayability.

It is not perfect. Missions can become repetitive, survivor dialogue and enclave behavior can feel limited, and after enough hours you start to notice where the systems could be deeper. I would love more meaningful relationships between survivors, more varied missions, deeper base customization, and smarter NPC behavior. But despite those flaws, the core gameplay loop is incredibly addictive. Few games make me care this much about individual survivors or make a simple supply run feel genuinely risky.

If you enjoy zombie survival, community management, exploration, and making your own stories, I absolutely recommend it. 1,000+ hours later, I’m still playing.

The original state of decay was one of my favorite games for a loooong time. I played it on the microsoft store and steam for a combined 300+ hours easily.

State of Decay 2 fundamentally identical in its mechanics and gameplay structure apart from the addition of the blood plague and some quality of life changes. The graphics look way better. The combat, vehicles and exploration all feel way better. The skill progression is fleshed out a little more. Survivors in your "party" can carry things for you. Idle survivors will go out on scavenging missions of their own accord occasionally. It no longer feels so much like the progression of the game revolves entirely around you and your actions.

It definitely has much more the survival feel to it. Cars being more scarce and requiring maintenance and refueling, rucksacks being slightly less common/predictable in their appearance, survivors being less systematic in the way you bring them into the fold.

My only grief is that it lacks a bit in the replayability department, purely because it is so similar to the previous game in actual mechanics and the "day to day" of the game.

If you consider going back to play state of decay ocasionally like I did for years, this is definitely a good purchase. If state of decay has lost it's charm for you completely, don't bother (or buy it on sale) because the new mechanics, gameplay, etc are not quite different enough. All in all:

As a game this gets a 5/5, if you haven't played state of decay before and you like zombie/survival/scavenging, give it a shot. You will probably like it.

As a sequel to state of decay, this gets a 3/5. Graphical improvements and gameplay depth make it a good sequel, but a lack of growth in the fundamental way the game is played, the objectives and mechanics prevent it from being a great sequel. What would I have liked to see? Hard to say, but I would have liked to see a bit more creativity for sure.

State of Decay, despite its flaws, remains one of my favorite games of all time. I had high hopes that State of Decay 2, especially with Microsoft's backing, would blow it out of the water.

Don't get me wrong, I really like State of Decay 2. However, it plays like a giant expansion of State of Decay, not a sequel. The same things that annoyed me about the first game: The absurdly low amount of stamina, the ridiculously limited storage space in some vehicles, and the complete inability to actually improve your base's defenses, are still very much present.

In a game that prides itself as a community-building, base-expanding game, it's unforgivable how little you can actually do in your own base. That would be fine if the bases looked the part. They don't. For example, on one map there's a church with really great walls--if you can't climb the wall, then zombies can't climb it--and it's got some decent build options. But in one corner of the courtyard there's a pretty white gazebo that you can do NOTHING with. You can't make it a part of your base, you can't remove it. It just sits there, needlessly taking up a space that any normal zombie-apocalypse survivor would make use of. A garden has to be put into a slot, but that same church has raised vegetation beds with shrubs in them. Why can't I garden there?

Unfortunately, NPC characters are still just as useless as ever. During zombie assaults on your base, they all seemingly cluster in the watchtowers while the zombies just flood in through the doors. Oh, and doors! No matter how nice your walls are at keeping out zombies, doors can't be locked or blocked, so the zombies always have a path in that you can do nothing about. Since your NPCs are too dumb to split up and cover each door, there's literally no way to keep zombies out of your base during these times.

What frustrates me is that these are things that were already stupid about State of Decay, things the community hated. Things that should have been fixed. No one expects a sedan to carry 50 rucksacks of goods. But a truck? That's what trucks were made for!

And is it too much to ask to be able to upgrade your walls and doors in your base? I'd personally rather have our base constantly mobbed by zombies that we had to fight our way through every time we need to leave the base. That would be fun. These 'Fortresses of Ineptitude' need to go.

I'm gonna play this game so much, and I'm gonna enjoy it the same way I enjoyed the first one. I'm downvoting it because it should have addressed the flaws of State of Decay, with all the time and money invested in developing it.

Do better with State of Decay 3, if that ever happens.
